Package org.aristonis.diwan.database.query

Class Builder

java.lang.Object
org.aristonis.diwan.database.query.Builder
Direct Known Subclasses:
JoinClause
public class Builder extends Object
Builds one query fluently, a hand port of Laravel's Illuminate\Database\Query\Builder. 

 String sql = db.table("users").select("id", "name").where("active", true).orderBy("name").toSql();
 // select "id", "name" from "users" where "active" = ? order by "name" asc

Method names and behavior follow Laravel. PHP's optional arguments become overloads: a two-argument where(column, value) compares with =, a nested group is a Consumer<Builder>, and a map of conditions is a Map. As in Laravel:

  • a null value with = or <=> becomes is null, and with != or <> becomes is not null; with any other known operator it is rejected;
  • an operator the builder and grammar do not know is taken as the value, compared with =, so an operator never reaches the SQL unchecked;
  • a negative limit is ignored and a negative offset becomes zero.

Values are always bound as ?; an Expression value is written as given. Identifiers are always quoted by the grammar. Methods ending in Raw write trusted SQL as given and must never receive user input. An enum value is bound by its name.

A subquery is a Builder, a Consumer<Builder> that fills a fresh one, or, where a method says so, trusted SQL text. It is copied or compiled when it is attached, with its bindings in the bucket of the clause that holds it, so changing it afterwards changes nothing here. Joins are JoinClauses; after the first union(Builder), orders, limit and offset apply to the whole union.

A builder is mutable and not safe to share between threads. Every method that returns Builder changes this builder and returns it. clone() gives an independent copy. Lists returned by the getters are unmodifiable views of a snapshot.

    • newInstance

      protected Builder newInstance()
      Creates the empty builder that clone() and newQuery() fill; a subclass returns its own type.
      Returns:
      a new, empty builder on the same connection, grammar and processor, never null

    • clone

      public Builder clone()
      Returns an independent copy: changing either builder, including a nested group, a join or a union, never changes the other. Joins, unions and subqueries are private copies that no builder ever changes, so the copy shares them and only the lists are copied.
      Overrides:
      clone in class Object
      Returns:
      the copy, never null

      public final LengthAwarePage paginate(int perPage, int page)

      Parameters:
      perPage - the rows per page, at least 1
      page - the page number, from 1
      Returns:

    • paginate

      public final LengthAwarePage paginate(int perPage, int page, List<String> columns)
      Returns one page of rows with the total. The total comes first, from AggregateQueries.getCountForPagination(); when it is 0 the rows are not read. The page reads limit perPage offset (page - 1) * perPage and is empty past the last page. Without an order the rows of a page are whatever the database returns first.
      Parameters:
      perPage - the rows per page, at least 1
      page - the page number, from 1
      columns - the columns to select when the query selects none, never null; empty selects every column
      Returns:
      the page, never null
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if columns or a column is null
      IllegalArgumentException - if perPage or page is below 1
      ArithmeticException - if the page's offset does not fit in an int
      QueryException - if the database refuses a query

    • cursorPaginate

      public final CursorPage cursorPaginate(int perPage, Cursor cursor, List<String> columns)
      Returns the page a cursor points to, reading by key position instead of by offset, so rows added or removed between requests never shift a page. The query's column orders are the key: the page after a cursor reads (c1 > ? or (c1 = ? and (c2 > ? ...))), with < for a descending column, and the page before it reads with every order flipped and gives the rows back in the query's order. A select alias ("users.id as uid" ordered by uid) is resolved to its column. perPage + 1 rows are read to know whether another page follows.
      Parameters:
      perPage - the rows per page, at least 1
      cursor - the cursor from an earlier page, null for the first page
      columns - the columns to select when the query selects none, never null; empty selects every column; the rows must hold every order column
      Returns:
      the page, never null
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if columns or a column is null
      IllegalArgumentException - if perPage is below 1, the cursor's parameters are not the query's order columns, or a row's order value cannot be kept in a Cursor
      IllegalStateException - if the query is not ordered by a column: "You must specify an orderBy clause when using this function."
      QueryException - if the database refuses the query
      API Note:
      The order columns should together be unique and never null: rows that tie on every order column, or hold null in one, can be skipped, as in Laravel. Order by a unique key last.

    • cursor

      public final QueryCursor<Map<String,Object>> cursor()
      Runs the query and streams its rows through a cursor, as Connection.cursor(String, List) describes: the cursor must be closed, best with try-with-resources, and closes itself after the last row. Unlike the page methods it needs no order. The rows are not passed through the Processor.

      The cursor holds its session until it is closed, so a long loop over it leaves a PostgreSQL connection idle in transaction. Writing through the same database inside the loop needs a second connection, and a pool of one deadlocks. Use lazy(int) for a slow loop or one that writes. 

      
 try (QueryCursor<Map<String, Object>> rows = db.table("orders").orderBy("id").cursor()) {
     for (Map<String, Object> row : rows) {
         export(row);
     }
 }
      Returns:
      the open cursor, never null
      Throws:
      IllegalStateException - if a cursor is already open on the connection's session, or the query has a row lock that needs a transaction and none is open
      UnsupportedOperationException - in pretend mode, or if the driver cannot stream
      QueryException - if the database refuses the query

    • insertOrIgnore

      public final int insertOrIgnore(List<? extends Map<String,?>> rows)
      Inserts several rows in one statement, skipping each that would break a unique or primary key constraint: insert or ignore on SQLite, on conflict do nothing on PostgreSQL. SQLite also ignores a failed not null or check constraint this way. No rows runs nothing and returns 0.

      The statement is one round trip and is never split. Its bindings are the row values, so the batch must stay under the driver's limit: 999 bindings on SQLite before 3.32 and 32766 after, 65535 on PostgreSQL. Beyond that the database refuses the statement; chunk the rows yourself, inside a transaction when the chunks must succeed together.

      Parameters:
      rows - the rows, never null, all with the same columns
      Returns:
      the number of rows inserted, as the connection reports it
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if rows or a row is null
      IllegalArgumentException - if the rows have different columns
      UnsupportedOperationException - if the grammar cannot ignore errors, as the base grammar cannot; nothing runs then
      IllegalStateException - if the query reads no table, as after SubqueryClauses.fromSub(org.aristonis.diwan.database.query.Builder, java.lang.String)
      QueryException - if the database refuses the insert

    • upsert

      public final int upsert(List<? extends Map<String,?>> rows, List<String> uniqueBy)
      Inserts the rows, and where a row conflicts on the unique columns, sets every column of the first row from the row that was refused. SQLite writes on conflict ... do update set "c" = "excluded"."c", as does PostgreSQL.

      The statement is one round trip and is never split. Its bindings are the row values, so the batch must stay under the driver's limit: 999 bindings on SQLite before 3.32 and 32766 after, 65535 on PostgreSQL. Beyond that the database refuses the statement; chunk the rows yourself, inside a transaction when the chunks must succeed together.

      Two rows of one batch with the same unique key behave differently: SQLite applies them in order, so the last one wins; PostgreSQL refuses the statement ("cannot affect row a second time"). Remove duplicate keys from the batch first.

      Parameters:
      rows - the rows, never null, all with the same columns, none empty
      uniqueBy - the columns of the unique index that decides a conflict, never null or empty; the database refuses the statement if no such unique index exists
      Returns:
      the number of rows written, as the connection reports it; 0 for no rows
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if an argument, a row or a name in uniqueBy is null
      IllegalArgumentException - if uniqueBy is empty, a row has no columns or the rows have different columns
      UnsupportedOperationException - if the grammar or the database version cannot upsert; SQLite older than 3.24, as in Android before API 30, refuses it; nothing runs then
      IllegalStateException - if the query reads no table, as after SubqueryClauses.fromSub(org.aristonis.diwan.database.query.Builder, java.lang.String)
      QueryException - if the database refuses the statement

      public final boolean updateOrInsert(Map<String,?> attributes)
      Updates the first row matching the attributes, or inserts the attributes. It reads, then writes, in two statements, so it is not atomic: two callers can both find no row and both insert, or one insert can fail on a unique index the other just filled. Wrap it in a transaction with a lock, or use WriteQueries.upsert(List, List) on a unique index, which is one atomic statement, when that matters.
      Parameters:
      attributes - the columns to match and to insert, never null
      Returns:
      true
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if attributes is null
      IllegalStateException - if the query reads no table, as after SubqueryClauses.fromSub(org.aristonis.diwan.database.query.Builder, java.lang.String)
      QueryException - if the database refuses a statement

    • updateOrInsert

      public final boolean updateOrInsert(Map<String,?> attributes, Map<String,?> values)
      Updates the first row matching the attributes with the values, or inserts the attributes merged with the values. It reads, then writes, in two statements, so it is not atomic; see WriteQueries.updateOrInsert(Map). The query's own conditions apply to the read and the update, and this builder is left unchanged.
      Parameters:
      attributes - the columns to match and to insert, never null
      values - the columns to set, never null; the value wins over an attribute of the same name on insert; empty leaves a found row as it is
      Returns:
      true when a row was inserted, or found and left as it is or changed; false when the update changed no row
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if an argument is null
      UnsupportedOperationException - if the query has joins and the grammar cannot update with joins
      IllegalStateException - if the query reads no table, as after SubqueryClauses.fromSub(org.aristonis.diwan.database.query.Builder, java.lang.String)
      QueryException - if the database refuses a statement

    • getCountForPagination

      public final long getCountForPagination()
      Counts the rows every page of PageQueries.paginate(int, int) would show together, as Laravel's getCountForPagination does, on a copy so the builder is unchanged.

      A query with groups or having clauses is counted as a subquery, without its orders, limit and offset: select count(*) as "aggregate" from (...) as "aggregate_table"; a grouped join that selects nothing selects its table's columns there. A query with unions is counted whole, without the union's own orders, limit and offset; each part keeps its own. Any other query is counted without its columns, orders, limit and offset. The row lock is left out.

      A SelectClauses.distinct() query without unions is counted as a subquery too, like a grouped one, so the total is the number of distinct rows. This departs from Laravel, which drops the columns and counts every matching row, giving a total that disagrees with the pages.

      Returns:
      the count, never negative
      Throws:
      QueryException - if the database refuses the query

    • sumDecimal

      public final BigDecimal sumDecimal(String column, int scale)
      Returns the sum of a column as an exact decimal at a scale, rounded half up; 0 at that scale when no row matches. SQLite sums a decimal column as a double, so 0.1 + 0.2 comes back as 0.30000000000000004; rounding the sum back to the scale removes that drift, and is exact while the sum has at most 15 significant digits. Other drivers return an exact sum that only gets its scale set.
      Parameters:
      column - the column name, never null
      scale - the digits after the point, 0 or more
      Returns:
      the sum at scale, never null
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if column is null
      IllegalArgumentException - if scale is negative or the sum is text that is not a number
      QueryException - if the database refuses the query

    • lock

      public final Builder lock(LockStrength strength, LockWait lockWait)
      Locks the selected rows. The lock replaces an earlier one, applies to the select only, and is left out of aggregates, exists and the count of a pagination. A union with a lock on any part is refused when compiled.

      PostgreSQL renders every combination and holds the lock until the transaction ends, so a locked select outside a transaction throws IllegalStateException. SQLite has no row locks: it ignores LockStrength.UPDATE and LockStrength.SHARE with LockWait.WAIT, and refuses any other combination.

      Parameters:
      strength - the strength, never null
      lockWait - what to do when the rows are locked, never null
      Returns:
      this builder
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if an argument is null

    • lock

      public final Builder lock(LockStrength strength, Duration timeout)
      Locks the selected rows and waits for a conflicting lock at most timeout. The select must run inside a transaction, where the limit applies to that statement; outside one it throws IllegalStateException. A timeout beyond that is refused, and a sub-millisecond timeout rounds up to one millisecond.

      PostgreSQL renders a plain lock and limits the wait with SET LOCAL lock_timeout before the select. SQLite refuses a timed lock with UnsupportedOperationException.

      Parameters:
      strength - the strength, never null
      timeout - the longest wait, never null, more than zero and at most Integer.MAX_VALUE milliseconds
      Returns:
      this builder
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if an argument is null
      IllegalArgumentException - if timeout is zero, negative or too long

    • whereIntegerInRaw

      public final Builder whereIntegerInRaw(String column, Collection<?> values)
      Adds a condition that a column is in a list of integers written into the SQL, not bound; an empty list matches no row.

      A port of Laravel's whereIntegerInRaw, used by eager loading to keep a long list of integer keys out of the binding limit. Laravel casts each value with (int), which turns any text into a number; here every value must be an exact integer, so nothing but digits can reach the SQL. Accepted: Byte, Short, Integer, Long, a BigInteger or a whole BigDecimal in the long range, and canonical decimal text such as "42" or "-7" (not "01", " 1", "1.0" or "-0").

      Parameters:
      column - the column name, never null
      values - the integer values, never null, copied
      Returns:
      this builder
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if an argument is null
      IllegalArgumentException - if a value is not an exact integer; the message names the value's position and type, never the value

    • whereInstantBetween

      public final Builder whereInstantBetween(String column, Instant from, Instant to)
      Adds a condition that a moment column lies in [from, to): at or after from and before to, in parentheses.

      This is the way to filter an instant column. Laravel's date wheres compare the stored text of a date and do not work on a column that stores a number of microseconds. The grammar converts each Instant to what its database stores, and a plain range can use an index on the column.

      Parameters:
      column - the column name, never null
      from - the first moment included, never null
      to - the first moment excluded, never null
      Returns:
      this builder
      Throws:
      NullPointerException - if an argument is null

    • groupWheresAt

      public Builder groupWheresAt(int index, boolean newSliceJoinsWithAnd)
      Regroups the where conditions around index. The conditions before it and the conditions from it on are two slices; a slice that holds an or becomes one nested group, so its or cannot widen the other slice. A slice without an or stays flat. Only the wheres list changes: the bindings keep their order.
      Parameters:
      index - where the second slice starts, from 0 to the number of wheres
      newSliceJoinsWithAnd - whether the second slice, when grouped, joins the first with and instead of its own first conjunction
      Returns:
      this builder
      Throws:
      IllegalArgumentException - if index is below 0 or above the number of wheres

    • toRawSql

      public final String toRawSql()
      Compiles the query with its bindings written in as literals, for display and logging only.

      Never run the result: escaping a literal is weaker than binding it. Literals assume standard SQL strings, where a backslash is an ordinary character, as on SQLite and on PostgreSQL with standard_conforming_strings on.

      Returns:
      the SQL with values inlined, never null
      Throws:
      UnsupportedOperationException - if the grammar does not support a clause or cannot write a binding as a literal
      IllegalArgumentException - if a string binding holds a NUL character
